content:
Hello! I heard that introductions were appreciated so I will say a little about myself.

I recently graduated with a BA in math and computer science, and am in the midst of a gap year, before I hopefully go on to study more math in grad school.

I have loved computers all my life, but only got into math during college. I fell in love with proofs very soon after being introduced to them in an algorithms class. The fact that any proof, no matter how large, could be broken down into a series of simple agreeable transformations reminded me a lot of what I liked about computers.

Much later I learned about Lean, and languages like it, and it seems to be the perfect combination of my interests. I am still very new, but in my primitive understanding, the modeling of true and false with "constructable" and "not constructable" changed how I think about proofs in general. The way that a function arrow can represent implication proofs and forall proofs is wonderful. And "false implies anything" being explained by the existence of empty functions is so cool as well.

I hope to go on to work with Lean in graduate school after my gap year. (If anyone has grad school recommendations for someone interested in this kind of formalization, please feel free to share!)
